# Directing: story or explainer

An **explainer** answers the viewer's question (how something works, why it happens, what a fact
means) and succeeds when the viewer can retell the mechanism afterwards, and wants to. A **story**
follows someone who wants something and succeeds when the viewer feels the turn. Either way, fix
the film in text before anything is drawn: it is the cheapest place to change it.

## Intake

Ask only what the request leaves open, together and with your recommendations: where it's posted
and who watches, the one thing the viewer should understand or feel, length and what must appear,
tone and films they admire.

## Find the pictures

The pictures are where the film is won. The user sees the results, not the steps.

1. **References.** When the topic has strong explainers or the user supplies a film, study how
   they pictured each claim and why it works; take ideas, not looks. A reference the user
   supplies comes first and is studied shot by shot.
2. **Brainstorm, in a fresh agent.** Give it this brief, filled in, and nothing else: no style,
   format, production rules, past-film bans or preferences of your own.
   > Here is a script [with what comes just before and after it]. For every claim or story
   > moment, write picture ideas that differ in kind (the literal picture, an everyday analogy, an
   > impossible or wacky one, a change of scale, a personified one, the one a kid would draw):
   > what we see, and what happens to it. Be as inventive as the idea allows: an idea wins
   > when a viewer understands the mechanism faster, or remembers it longer, than with the
   > literal picture. [Reference notes, if any.] [The user's stated rules, verbatim, if any.]
3. **Pick, in a second fresh agent.**
   > Here are picture ideas for a script. Judge each for clarity (with the sound off, could a
   > viewer infer the mechanism?), surprise (would someone screenshot it?) and spectacle (does
   > the motion itself hold the eye: scale, many parts moving together, light? one line or one
   > drifting object is thin), and what it costs to build in [the time and route]. Pick one per
   > beat, combining ideas when that beats both. The literal picture wins only when it is at
   > least as clear and as surprising as the best alternative. Then check the picks as a set:
   > they should feel like one film, so a change of world earns its place, and a device that
   > links sections connects the beats' own pictures. Give your reasoning and the runners-up for
   > the biggest beats.
4. For the beats the film will be remembered for, let the user pick from rendered directions
   (stills and a little motion), not descriptions.

## Concepts and beat sheet

Pitch concepts built from the picks that differ in world, angle or shape, at least one of them
bold, each with the pictures for its key beats. Develop the chosen one into a beat sheet timed to
the length that gives every line its picture and the event in it. A line with nothing to show is
a candidate for the narrator on camera, a caption, or a cut. At 30 seconds a story is one small
arc, not an epic.

## Checks, before you show it

Explainer:
- The opening question is concrete and answered by the end.
- Every term is defined in words a newcomer follows; numbers on screen equal the narration's.
- Each line has a picture that is an event. A shot whose only change is ambient drift while the
  voice explains is a hold, not a beat.
- Any visual code (a colour, a shape or a position that carries meaning) is shown once in a
  legible image before it is used.

Story:
- The protagonist wants something and makes the decisive choice.
- Something is in the way and the middle escalates; scenery is not a beat.
- The turn is unexpected but believable.
- The payoff reads at phone size in one look; if it needs a close-up, the close-up is its own
  beat.
- One specific, surprising detail beats generic charm.

## Alignment stop

Present the concepts with your recommendation and the recommended one's beat sheet with its
pictures, so the user can approve in one reply. Silence is not approval. When the user supplied a
finished story or said to go ahead without reviewing, still run the checks and name any weakness
in one line.
